beats.care: A weaker rupee makes imported things cost more, from petrol and phones to studying abroad. RBI is trying to slow that slide.
beats.what: From today, RBI will sell dollars directly to Indian Oil, HPCL and BPCL, covering all their daily dollar needs.
beats.why: The rupee closed at 96.71 to the dollar on Friday. Oil companies buying huge amounts of dollars in the market pushes it lower.

cards.body: The rupee opened at 95.75 on Monday, up 98 paise from Friday, and stayed near 95.80. One analyst calls it a near-term positive, but crude above $100 and foreign investors pulling money out still weigh on it.
cards.title: 🆕 Evening update

cards.body: Oil companies pay for crude in dollars, roughly $300 million a day per The Hindu. Normally they buy those dollars from the market, which drags the rupee down. Now RBI will sell to them through chosen banks, starting 12 October, until further notice.
RBI cut the amount firms can hedge without showing a real need from $100 million to $5 million, to curb betting against the rupee.
cards.caption: New limit for hedging without proof

cards.body: India imports most of its oil and lots of electronics. When one dollar costs more rupees, all of those cost more too. That feeds inflation, which is why RBI raised interest rates last week.
cards.title: why does a weak rupee hurt you?

cards.body: This isn't new. RBI opened a similar special dollar window for oil companies in August 2013, during an earlier rupee crash.

opts: Yes, a falling rupee hurts everyone
cards.q: Should RBI spend India's dollar savings to defend the rupee?

opts: So their big dollar buying doesn't push the rupee down further
Because oil companies ran out of rupees
cards.q: Why is RBI selling dollars directly to oil companies?
cards.why: Taking the oil firms' huge dollar demand out of the market eases pressure on the rupee.
